n: The father begins a lesson on sexual morality, calling his son to listen closely.

f.g: Lean in and listen carefully.

n: The goal is that the son will keep good judgment and speak with knowledge rather than be led by smooth talk.

f.g: discretion = careful judgment, thoughtful planning.

n: The adulteress’s words seem sweet as dripping honey and smoother than olive oil. Temptation always looks attractive at first.

f.g: An adulteress—a woman outside one’s marriage covenant.

n: But the aftertaste is bitter and the outcome cuts like a sword. Sin promises sweetness and delivers pain.

f.g: wormwood = a very bitter plant, a symbol of bitterness and sorrow.

n: Her path leads straight down to death and the grave.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol—the grave, the realm of the dead.

n: She never thinks about the path of life; her ways wander and she doesn’t even know it. Her life is unstable and aimless.

f.g: Her ways wander, unsteady and shifting.

n: The father pleads again with all his children to hold on to his words.

f.w: depart not from the words of my mouth

n: The best defense: stay far away. Don’t even go near her door.

f.w: come not nigh the door of her house
f.g: nigh = near.

n: Adultery can cost your honor and the best years of your life, handing them to people who will show no mercy.

f.g: Possibly an angry husband or others who exploit the offender.

n: Strangers may end up enjoying the wealth you worked for. Infidelity brings real financial and family costs.

f.g: The fruits of your hard work.

n: At the end of life, the man who chose this path groans as his body wastes away—perhaps through disease or simply in old-age regret.

f.g: Or “groan.”

n: His regret is spoken aloud: why did I hate correction and despise warnings?
He admits he refused to listen to those who tried to teach him.

f.g: Listened attentively.

n: He came close to complete ruin in front of the whole community—public disgrace was one of the consequences.

f.g: The gathered community, possibly where cases were judged.

n: Now the positive side: find joy in your own spouse. Water from your own cistern and well is a poetic image of marital love.

f.g: cistern = a stone-cut tank for collecting rainwater—precious in a dry land.

n: A rhetorical question in many translations: should your springs overflow into the streets? The meaning is that your love should not be scattered abroad.

f.w: Let thy fountains be dispersed abroad
f.g: Many translators read this as a question: “Should your springs be scattered abroad?”

n: Keep your love for your spouse alone, not shared with strangers.

f.w: Let them be only thine own

n: May your marriage be blessed. Rejoice in the wife you married when young—fidelity is meant to be a source of joy, not just duty.

f.w: rejoice with the wife of thy youth

n: Frank and tender poetry celebrates married love. The doe and gazelle were images of grace and beauty. God intends husband and wife to delight in each other.

f.g: hind = a female deer, a doe.
roe = a gazelle or small deer.
ravished = captivated, intoxicated with delight.

n: So why be captivated by another man’s wife? The question shows how foolish it is to trade a faithful love for a forbidden one.

f.w: embrace the bosom of a stranger

n: Nothing is hidden. The Lord sees every path a person takes and weighs every step.

f.w: before the eyes of the LORD

f.g: pondereth = weighs, examines carefully.

n: The wicked get trapped by their own sins, tied up as if by ropes. Sin binds the one who commits it.

f.g: holden = held.

n: He dies because he refused discipline, staggering off course in his great foolishness.

f.g: Hebrew word also used in verse 19 for being “ravished”—a wordplay: captivated by folly instead of love.
